auth.notes: Okta OIDC against auth.hyperice.com, then a token exchange at POST app.hyperice.com/v1/auth/okta-token-exchange mints the JWT every other call needs. Unauthenticated probes return 401 INVALID_JWT.

data_leaves_device: routine usage / completion sync (phone-side; the BLE device itself has no network interface)

endpoints.returns: Device catalog entries carrying firmwareVersion and firmwareUrl fields.
Guided 'HyperSmart' routine library (auto-adjusts speed during a session).

Request body is a list of {deviceId, version, type, submodel?}; response is {url, hash, version, deviceId, type}. Requires a valid account JWT (401 without); no firmware URLs are hardcoded in the app. NOTE: the legacy Hypervolt family has no in-app OTA path anyway, so this endpoint matters to the newer families, not to this device.

cloud.failure_mode: Nothing on the device stops working. All control is local BLE, and the gun also runs standalone from its physical speed button. What dies with the cloud is phone-side: account login, the guided routine library and routine-completion sync, and firmware-update metadata for the newer families. Confirmed alive 2026-08-18 (unauthenticated calls return 401).
cloud.notes: Endpoint set and auth shape read from the vendor Android app. Other app-side dependencies seen: Firebase (Realtime Database, FCM, Analytics), Amplitude, Sentry, and Lokalise for OTA string translations.

identity.notes: Whether the BLE address is public or rotates was not established from the app; if a unit turns out to use a resolvable private address, key on the local name instead (it carries the model prefix).

manufacturer_data.description: Hyperice manufacturer data under Bluetooth SIG company ID 0x08BA.

Hyperice's Bluetooth SIG company identifier, listed by the research as used in this product line's advertising. The app itself matches on the advertised local-name prefix, so the company ID is a secondary signal.

device.name: Hyperice Hypervolt Plus
device.notes:
Hypervolt Plus (Bluetooth) — 90 W percussion massage gun, 3 speeds, 5 heads, model 54020 001-00 per the device.report listing. One spec covers the whole "legacy" Hypervolt family sharing one GATT layout and one app manager: Hypervolt, Hypervolt Plus, Hypervolt 2, Hypervolt 2 Pro, and the Vyper 3 / Vyper Go rollers. Hyperice is alive and healthy (Hypervolt 3 line launched March 2026); there is no cloud-shutdown risk today, and — more to the point — the device needs no cloud at all: all control is local BLE.
App taxonomy (device-type model numbers, from the vendor app): HYPERVOLT=1, HYPERVOLT_PLUS=2, HYPERVOLT_2=5, HYPERVOLT_2_PRO=6, VYPER_GO=3, VYPER_3=4. Advertised local-name prefixes are matched case-insensitively and END IN A SEMICOLON: `HV;` Hypervolt, `HV+;` Hypervolt Plus, `HV2;` / `HV2P;` Hypervolt 2 / 2 Pro, `VY3;` / `VYGO;` Vyper 3 / Go. Bluetooth SIG company IDs seen in this product line's advertising: 2234 (0x08BA) = Hyperice; 89 (0x0059) = Nordic Semiconductor (seen on the Normatec 2 family, likely DFU-mode adverts).
The BLE core of the app still lives in the package namespace of RelaxRoll, the company Hyperice acquired — the 2019-era RelaxRoll "Hyperice" app is superseded by a single unified Hyperice app.
Not present on this family: no battery characteristic (battery shows on the device's LED ring only), and no OTA/DFU characteristic — the legacy manager has no firmware-update path at all (its update routine is a no-op). Newer Hyperice families in the same app (Hypervolt 3, Normatec, Venom 2, Hyperice X) use different UUID bases and Nordic DFU and are NOT covered here.
Open questions (need hardware): 1. Does the secure characteristic's seed read back 00 00 00 on a fresh
   unit (making the password write unnecessary), or a random seed per
   connection?
2. Exact level range/semantics: expected 0-3 (off + 3 speeds); unverified
   whether notifications echo the speed or a force-sensor pressure band.
3. The containing GATT service UUID for the two custom characteristics is
   not pinned in the app (it matches characteristics by UUID only) — the
   service UUID recorded below is an inference, not an observation.
4. The Hypervolt Plus-specific FCC ID (grantee code for Hyperice is
   2AY3Y, per sibling products' filings).

issued_to_client: 4-byte session password derived from the device MAC and seed (written back, not stored)
stored_on_device: Session seed served by the secure characteristic (per research; whether it is static or per-connection is unknown)

factory_reset.effect: No factory-reset procedure was found in the app for this family, and the pairing model (a per-connection derived password, not a stored bond) suggests there may be no persistent pairing state to clear. Unknown whether a button-combination reset exists on the hardware.

ble.pin_source: None — no BLE bonding; authorization is the derived-password write on the secure characteristic.

methods.description: Scan for the `HV+;` name prefix, connect, run the seed/password handshake, then subscribe to the level characteristic and write single-byte levels. The app's own connection builder uses a 15 s timeout with 7 retries.

steps.action: Scan for a BLE peripheral whose local name starts with HV+; (case-insensitive).
steps.expect: Advertisement with local name HV+;… (and typically Hyperice company ID 0x08BA).

steps.action: Read the secure characteristic and take its last 3 bytes as the session seed.
steps.expect: A value whose last 3 bytes are the seed; 00 00 00 means no password is needed.

steps.action: If the seed is nonzero, write the derived 4-byte password back to the secure characteristic (write with response).
steps.notes: Derivation documented on the characteristic below; it mixes the device MAC with the seed through a fixed 256-entry lookup table recovered from the app. Structure ({0x01, b1, b2, b3}, the seed read, the table) is certain; bit-mixing details are a register-level transcription — verify against hardware.

steps.action: Subscribe to notifications on the level characteristic.
steps.expect: Notifications carrying the current level as a single byte.

setup.notes: Nothing to provision — no network, no account, no cloud. The gun works standalone from its physical speed button; BLE adds app control. The one complication is the per-connection handshake on the "secure" characteristic: after connecting, read the 3-byte seed from 31CB4570-..., and unless the seed is 00 00 00 (in which case nothing is written), derive the 4-byte password documented on that characteristic and write it back with response. Confidence is low because the flow was read from the app's dispatch code, not replayed against a device.

rejoin.notes: BLE-only device with no network binding: a new phone/controller simply scans, connects and runs the handshake. The realistic failure mode is another client still holding the single BLE connection — close the vendor app before expecting a third-party client to connect.

testing.notes: No hardware has been driven from this spec. Every protocol fact below was recovered by static analysis of the vendor Android app (2026-08); the cloud host was probed unauthenticated only (returned HTTP 401, i.e. alive). The password-derivation bit mixing in particular is a register-level transcription and is marked hypothesis pending a hardware check.

entities.name: Percussion Level
entities.notes: 0 = off, 1-3 = the gun's three hardware speeds (expected range, not wire-verified). State arrives via notifications on the same characteristic; whether it echoes the commanded speed or a pressure band is an open question.

local_access.summary: Full local control over BLE as shipped: scan for the `HV+;` name prefix, connect, run the seed/password handshake on the secure characteristic, then write single-byte levels and read level notifications. No account, no cloud, no DNS redirect. An esphome_ble_client or Home Assistant BLE integration is straightforward once the handshake is implemented — and may be trivial if fresh units answer the seed read with 00 00 00 (unverified).

write_password.description: Write the derived 4-byte session password {0x01, b1, b2, b3}. b1-b3 are computed from the device MAC and the seed just read from this same characteristic — they are not user-settable, so a generic consumer cannot emit this command without implementing the derivation in the notes above.

b1.description: Derived byte 1 (see derivation in characteristic notes).

b2.description: Derived byte 2 (see derivation in characteristic notes).

b3.description: Derived byte 3 (see derivation in characteristic notes).

format.name: seed
format.notes: The LAST 3 bytes of the read value are the seed; the read value may be longer (its leading bytes were not characterized). All zero means no password required this session.

characteristics.name: Secure (seed read / password write)
characteristics.notes:
Read yields a value whose LAST 3 bytes are the session seed (s[0..2]). If the seed is 00 00 00, no password is written (the app writes an empty array). Otherwise the app derives a 4-byte password P = {0x01, b1, b2, b3} from the seed and the device MAC (mac[0..5]) and writes it back WITH RESPONSE (write type 2). Derivation, transcribed from the app's bytecode (uses a fixed 256-entry lookup table T stored in the app, beginning 1,128,64,32,16,8,132,66,33,144,72,164,…):

  A  = s[0] ^ mac[5]
  b1 = (((mac[5] | mac[1]) & 0xff) ^ T[(mac[4] ^ s[2]) & 0xff]) >> (s[2] & 1)
  b2 = s[2] ^ ((T[(mac[2] & s[1]) & 0xff] + mac[3]) & 0xffff)
  b3 = ((mac[0] ^ T[A & 0xff]) & 0xff) << (s[1] & 1)

with results truncated to bytes. The full table T is recoverable from the vendor app (see sources). STRUCTURE CERTAIN (4-byte password headed 0x01, 3-byte seed, table-driven mixing); BIT-MIXING DETAILS HYPOTHESIS — verify against hardware before trusting an implementation.

set_level.description: Set the percussion level (single byte, written without response). Hypervolt Plus hardware has 3 speeds, so expect 0-3 (0 = off); the upper bound is unverified and other family variants (e.g. Vyper rollers) may accept a wider range.

level.description: Percussion level; 0 = off. Max of 3 is expected from the hardware spec, not wire-verified.

stop.description: Stop the motor / reset the level to 0.

format.name: level
format.notes: Notification payload: current level as one integer byte. Exact semantics (commanded speed vs. pressure band) unverified.

characteristics.name: Level Control
characteristics.notes: Single-byte level in both directions. Writes (without response, write type 1) set the percussion level; notifications report the current level back to the app, parsed as one integer byte. Whether the notification echoes the commanded speed or a force-sensor pressure band is unverified (open question). Level range expected 0-3 on the Hypervolt Plus (off + its 3 hardware speeds) — unverified.

services.name: Hypervolt Legacy Service
services.notes: HYPOTHESIS (like the jlx-laser-distance-meter spec): the containing service UUID is not pinned anywhere in the app — it discovers services and matches the two characteristics below by UUID alone. 31cb4500 is inferred from the shared 31CB45xx base of the characteristic UUIDs and must be confirmed with a scan; clients should match the characteristics, not this service.

sources.description: Static analysis of the vendor Android app (2026-08). Obfuscated, but every relevant BLE class reads cleanly. Source of the two custom characteristic UUIDs and the DIS UUIDs, the fixed 256-entry password lookup table, the password-derivation routine, and the legacy Hypervolt family device manager whose dispatch defines the command set.
Unauthenticated probe 2026-08-18 returned 401 INVALID_JWT — cloud alive, JWT-gated.
